summary: Defines the IANA Charset MIB, with a textual convention called IANACharset for naming character sets in MIB objects. It is now an IANA registry and was extracted from Printer MIB v2 (RFC 3805). It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a list of names of text alphabets and codes that device dashboards can use to say what text format they use.

questions: how do network devices specify character encoding
subtitle: A standard naming convention for character encodings in network device management.

tldr.problem: Network devices need to report what text encodings they support when accessed via SNMP, but there was no standard way for MIB modules to specify character set labels.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3808 defines a textual convention called IANACharset that uses the IANA Charset Registry to provide a standard enumeration of character set names and codes that MIB modules can reference.
tldr.outcome: Device management systems can now consistently specify and negotiate character encodings, supporting everything from ASCII to UTF-8 to vendor-specific charsets, and the standard can be automatically updated when IANA registers new charsets.

today: RFC 3808 is an Informational document that is now an IANA registry. The IANACharset textual convention is an IANA-maintained standard that continues to support legacy SNMP-managed devices that need to specify their character encoding. The IANA Charset MIB can be automatically regenerated as new charsets are registered in accordance with RFC 2978.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets network administrators manage devices like printers and switches via a virtual database called the MIB (Management Information Base). Objects in the MIB are defined using SMI (Structure of Management Information).

RFC 3808 defines a single textual convention called IANACharset for use in MIB modules. A textual convention is a reusable data type. The IANACharset convention lets MIB objects specify character set labels in a standard way. It was extracted from the Printer MIB and originally appeared (misnamed as CodedCharSet) in RFC 1759.
sections.eli5: When you connect to a device to manage it, you need to say what text alphabet it uses. This defines a standard list of alphabet names so the device and your computer speak the same language.

sections.title: The IANACharset Textual Convention
sections.content:
The IANACharset textual convention is an INTEGER that references the IANA Charset Registry (maintained at http://www.iana.org/assignments/character-sets). Each charset has two identifiers: an enumeration value (the MIBenum field in the registry) and an enumeration label (derived from the Alias field that begins with "cs").

The convention includes common charsets: ASCII (csASCII), ISO Latin variants (csISOLatin1 through csISOLatin6), Unicode variants (csUnicode, csUTF8, csUTF16), and many vendor-specific and regional charsets. Two special values exist: "other" (value 1) for unregistered charsets and "unknown" (value 2) as a default. MIB objects such as prtLocalizationCharacterSet (console text), prtInterpreterDefaultCharSetIn (received print data), and prtInterpreterDefaultCharSetOut (output data) use this convention to specify what text encoding they use.
sections.eli5: It is a numbered list of text alphabets with standard names, so when a device says "I use csUTF8," everyone knows it means UTF-8 text.

sections.title: Machine Generation and Maintenance
sections.content:
The RFC includes a C language utility called ianachar.c that can automatically regenerate the IANACharset textual convention when IANA updates the Charset Registry. The utility parses the registry, extracting the charset Name field, the MIBenum value (IANA-assigned decimal number), and the Alias field prefixed with "cs". If no alias is found, it constructs one from the Name field by preserving only alphanumeric characters and prefixing with "cs".

The tool and its template file were donated to IANA in perpetuity without restriction. The RFC recommends that future updates to the IANA Charset MIB be machine-generated rather than hand-edited to prevent inconsistency between the registry and the MIB. The MIB module was last updated in June 2004 based on the registry at that time.
sections.eli5: When IANA adds a new text alphabet to its list, a computer program automatically adds it to this standard list, so devices can use it without waiting for people to edit things by hand.

sections.title: Best Practices and Internationalization
sections.content:
RFC 3808 notes that modern MIB modules should prefer SnmpAdminString (defined in RFC 3411), which always uses UTF-8, rather than relying on variable character sets. This aligns with the IETF Policy on Character Sets and Languages (RFC 2277).

However, IANACharset is valuable for legacy devices and situations where devices support multiple character encodings. The textual convention supports internationalization: device dashboards and management interfaces can use the IANACharset values to label and negotiate text encoding with network-managed devices, ensuring that characters in device names, descriptions, and configuration data are properly interpreted regardless of language or region.
sections.eli5: New devices should just use UTF-8 (a universal text code). But for older devices that speak many languages, this list lets them tell your computer what language they are using.
